questions.stem: Choose the correct form to complete the sentence: 'If I ______ the answer, I would have told you immediately.'

options.option_text: know (present tense — wrong for a past hypothetical)
knew (past simple — this is the Type 2 form, not Type 3 past perfect)
had known (past perfect — correct for Type 3 conditional with past hypothetical)
would know (modal + base — modal in the if-clause is non-standard)

questions.explanation: C is correct. The sentence expresses a hypothetical past situation (I didn't know the answer). This is a Type 3 conditional: If + past perfect (had + V3), ... would have + V3. Main clause 'would have told' confirms the Type 3 structure. 'Knew' (B) is Type 2 (present hypothetical). 'Would know' (D) is incorrect because modals do not go in the if-clause.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'If water ______ to 100°C, it boils.'

options.option_text: is heated (present simple — correct for Type 0 universal truth)
was heated (past simple — implies hypothetical, wrong for a scientific fact)
were heated (subjunctive past — reserved for hypotheticals, not facts)
would be heated (modal in if-clause — grammatically incorrect)

questions.explanation: A is correct. This is a Type 0 (Zero) conditional expressing a universal or scientific truth. Structure: If + present simple, present simple. 'If water is heated to 100°C, it boils' — always true. B and C create hypothetical conditions using past forms, which are inappropriate for established facts. D (modal in the if-clause) is always grammatically non-standard.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'If he ______ harder, he might pass the examination next month.'

options.option_text: studied (past simple — Type 2 form; 'might pass' in main clause confirms Type 2)
studies (present simple — Type 1 would use 'will pass', not 'might pass')
had studied (past perfect — would require 'might have passed' in main clause)
would study (modal in if-clause — non-standard)

questions.explanation: A is correct. The main clause uses 'might pass' (modal + base), which signals Type 2 conditional (present/future hypothetical). Type 2: If + past simple, would/might/could + base. 'If he studied harder' (he probably doesn't study hard enough currently), 'he might pass next month'. C (past perfect + might have passed) would refer to a past missed opportunity — not 'next month'. B (studies) with 'might pass' is not the standard Type 1 pattern.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'Unless you ______ on time, the presentation will start without you.'

options.option_text: arrive (present simple — 'unless' = 'if not'; Type 1 conditional)
arrived (past simple — creates Type 2 which would need 'would start', not 'will start')
will arrive (future in unless-clause — non-standard; unless takes present, not future)
don't arrive (double negative — 'unless' already has negative meaning)

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Unless' means 'if not'. Type 1 structure: Unless + present simple, will + base. 'Unless you arrive on time, the presentation will start without you.' B (arrived) is past simple — used in Type 2, but main clause 'will start' is Type 1. C (will arrive) — the unless/if-clause does not take the future tense even when referring to future. D creates a double negative: 'unless you don't arrive' = 'if you don't not arrive' = 'if you arrive' — opposite meaning.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'I wish I ______ a better command of English when I was in school.'

options.option_text: have (present simple — 'I wish' + present is non-standard for past regret)
had (past simple — 'I wish' + past simple expresses present wish, not past regret)
had had (past perfect — correct: 'I wish' + past perfect = regret about past)
would have (modal + base — 'I wish + would' = regret about current habits, not past)

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'I wish' + past perfect (had + V3) expresses regret about something in the past. 'When I was in school' confirms this is about the past. 'I wish I had had a better command' — double 'had' looks unusual but is grammatically correct: first 'had' is the auxiliary, second 'had' is the main verb (to have). Option B ('had') would mean 'I wish I had [now]' — a present wish. Option D ('would have') is sometimes used for regret but less standard.

questions.stem: Identify the TYPE of conditional in this sentence: 'If the satellite had been launched on schedule, the mission would have been accomplished by now.'

options.option_text: Type 0 (Zero conditional — used for universal truths)
Type 1 (First conditional — real and likely future situations)
Type 2 (Second conditional — present/future hypothetical)
Type 3 (Third conditional — past hypothetical with past perfect in if-clause)

questions.explanation: D is correct. Type 3 conditional structure: If + past perfect (had been launched), ... would have + past participle (would have been accomplished). This expresses an unreal or hypothetical past situation — the satellite was NOT launched on schedule, so the mission was NOT accomplished. Key markers: 'had been' (past perfect) in the if-clause and 'would have been' in the main clause.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'Provided that all members ______ their dues, the conference will proceed as planned.'

options.option_text: pay (present simple — 'provided that' functions like Type 1 if-clause)
paid (past simple — creates Type 2 but 'will proceed' is Type 1 main clause)
will pay (future in the if-clause — non-standard with 'provided that')
would pay (modal in condition clause — grammatically incorrect)

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Provided that' is a conditional conjunction equivalent to 'if'. Type 1 structure: Provided that + present simple, will + base. 'Provided that all members pay their dues, the conference will proceed.' B (paid) clashes with 'will proceed' in the main clause. C (will pay) — condition clauses don't take future tense even when referring to the future. D (would pay) is a modal in the condition clause, which is non-standard.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form to fill in both blanks: 'If I ______ you, I ______ that contract immediately.'

options.option_text: am / will reject (Type 1 — possible but 'were' is preferred for 'if I were you' idiom)
was / would reject (past simple — Type 2 but standard idiom uses 'were' not 'was')
were / would reject (subjunctive 'were' — standard form for Type 2 advice/hypothetical)
had been / would have rejected (Type 3 — past perfect; this is a present advice sentence)

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'If I were you' is the standard English subjunctive form for advice or hypothetical identification — it uses 'were' for ALL persons (not 'was'). Main clause: 'would + base' confirming Type 2. The full sentence: 'If I were you, I would reject that contract immediately.' Option B (was) is sometimes heard in informal speech but is considered grammatically incorrect in formal/exam contexts. D (had been / would have rejected) refers to a past hypothetical, not present advice.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'Had he informed us in advance, we ______ appropriate arrangements.'

options.option_text: would make (simple modal — incompatible with past hypothetical 'had he informed')
will have made (future perfect — wrong tense for Type 3)
would have made (modal + have + V3 — correct main clause for inverted Type 3)
would be making (modal + progressive — wrong aspect for completed past arrangements)

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Had he informed us' is an inverted Type 3 conditional (no 'if', subject-auxiliary inverted). It equals 'If he had informed us'. Main clause: 'would have + past participle'. Full: 'Had he informed us in advance, we would have made appropriate arrangements.' Option A (would make) is Type 2 — clashes with the past perfect in the condition. D (would be making) suggests an ongoing action, not a completed arrangement.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence that uses a MIXED conditional (referring to a past condition with a present result).

options.option_text: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic. (Type 1 — both clauses future)
If he had studied medicine, he would be a doctor now. (past condition, present result — mixed)
If she worked harder, she would earn more. (Type 2 — both clauses present hypothetical)
If they had left earlier, they would have caught the train. (Type 3 — both clauses past)

questions.explanation: B is correct. A mixed conditional combines: If + past perfect (past condition) ... would + base (present result). 'If he had studied medicine' (past — he didn't) + 'he would be a doctor now' (present consequence). This differs from Type 3 because the result refers to the PRESENT ('now'), not the past ('would have been'). Options A (Type 1), C (Type 2), and D (Type 3) are all standard conditionals — none of them mixed.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly formed conditional sentence:

options.option_text: If she will call me, I will pick her up from the station. (will in if-clause — non-standard)
If I were taller, I would have joined the police force last year. (Type 2+Type 3 mix — inconsistent)
If the power goes out, charge your devices in advance. (Type 0/advice conditional — correct)
Had I known, I will inform you. (inverted past perfect + will — inconsistent tense)

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'If the power goes out, charge your devices in advance' uses the imperative in the main clause — a valid construction for advice/commands. Structure: If + present simple, imperative. This is a Type 1-adjacent conditional giving advice. A (will in if-clause) is a common mistake — the if-clause takes present, not future. B mixes Type 2 condition ('were') with Type 3 result ('would have joined') — inconsistent. D mixes an inverted Type 3 condition ('Had I known') with a Type 1 result ('will inform') — tenses clash.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'Even if it ______ tomorrow, the outdoor event will not be cancelled.'

options.option_text: rains (present simple — correct: 'even if' + present simple, will + base)
will rain (future — non-standard in even-if/if clauses)
rained (past simple — would create Type 2, needing 'would not be cancelled')
had rained (past perfect — would create Type 3 with 'would not have been cancelled')

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Even if' is a concessive conditional — it introduces a condition that doesn't change the outcome. Structure follows Type 1: even if + present simple, will + base. 'Even if it rains tomorrow, the event will not be cancelled.' B (will rain) puts a future modal in the condition clause — not standard. C (rained) + 'will not be cancelled' creates a Type 1/Type 2 mismatch. D (had rained) is past perfect and would need 'would not have been cancelled' in the main clause.
